title: How long are the eraser, the pencil and the chalk?
description: An eraser, a pencil and a chalk lie along a ruler with ten parts in every centimetre. For each one the whole centimetres are read first and the parts after the mark are counted as tenths. Keeko doubts the eraser and writes the centimetres and the parts side by side.
teaching_notes: One idea: a length is the whole centimetres first, and then the tenths counted after the mark. Watch for students who write the two numbers side by side, so that two and four become twenty four.

source: Along a ruler marked in tenths of a centimetre, an eraser ends 4 parts after the 2 cm mark, a pencil ends 5 parts after the 4 cm mark and a chalk ends 4 parts after the 1 cm mark. Write each length.
video_script.why: The child has met a length as whole centimetres and tenths and now writes the lengths of three everyday objects.
video_script.substitution: Read the whole centimetres first, then count the parts after the mark as tenths of a centimetre.
video_script.anchor: An eraser, a pencil and a chalk along a ruler with ten equal parts in every centimetre
video_script.wrong_move: Keeko writes the 2 cm and the 4 parts side by side as 24 cm, but the eraser ends only a little past the 2 cm mark, so the bubble is struck.
video_script.payoff_line: The eraser is two and four tenths centimetres

final_answer.value: Eraser 2 4/10 cm, pencil 4 5/10 cm (4 1/2 cm), chalk 1 4/10 cm
final_answer.spoken: the eraser is two and four tenths centimetres, the pencil is four and five tenths centimetres, and the chalk is one and four tenths centimetres

maths_rules: Each cm is split into 10 equal parts, so one part is 1/10 cm.
Eraser: 2 whole cm and 4 parts of 1/10 cm, so 2 4/10 cm.
Pencil: 4 whole cm and 5 parts of 1/10 cm, so 4 5/10 cm; 5/10 is half, so 4 5/10 = 4 1/2 cm.
Chalk: 1 whole cm and 4 parts of 1/10 cm, so 1 4/10 cm.
Slip: writing 2 and 4 side by side gives 24 cm, far past the eraser's real end.
video_script.design: One idea: a length is the whole centimetres first and the tenths after them. Assumes the child has seen one part as one tenth of a centimetre. Wrong idea: write the centimetres and the parts side by side. The ruler with the three objects stays all video.

narration: <bookmark mark='doubt'/>Keeko thinks the eraser is twenty four centimetres, because the numbers are two and four.
<bookmark mark='fix'/>But the eraser ends only a little past the two mark. The four counts small parts, so it means four tenths and not four more centimetres.
